reponse:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cascade gains as a function of context length in retrieval-augmented generation
PROPOSAL: We ask how the benefit of a self-draft level above prompt lookup depends on how much context the lookup can mine. On retrieval-augmented question answering built from Natural Questions with a varying number of retrieved passages, and on long-document summarisation, we run Llama-2-13B-chat and Qwen2-7B-instruct with prompt lookup alone and with a layer-skipping self-draft above it, binning results by prompt length, and we report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and acceptance per level per bin.
CONTROLS: Autoregressive decoding and lookup alone per bin, the self-draft alone per bin, a cascade with the lookup window restricted to the generated text only, swept draft lengths, repeated timings, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: We expect lookup acceptance to rise with context length and the self-draft level to matter only on the shortest prompts, so the cascade's gain over lookup alone should shrink to nothing beyond a few thousand tokens of context. The restricted-window cascade should show where the lookup gain comes from.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Position-dependent drafting without training, a horizontal cascade of self-draft and lookup
PROPOSAL: We test the horizontal idea that the first positions of a draft block deserve the more accurate drafter. Within each speculation round, the opening draft tokens come from an early-exit self-draft that runs the target model up to an intermediate layer and reuses the final normalisation and unembedding, and the remaining tokens of the block come from n-gram lookup in the prompt and generated prefix. We move the split point from the start to the end of the block on Vicuna-7B and Llama-3-8B-instruct over the six Spec-Bench categories and we measure speedup over autoregressive decoding together with the mean number of accepted tokens per round.
CONTROLS: The comparison includes early-exit drafting alone and lookup alone at the same total block length, the reversed arrangement where lookup drafts the opening positions, a cascade whose drafter is chosen at random per position, and a sweep of the block length so that the best fixed schedule for each single drafter is known before the mixed schedule is judged, with outputs checked against greedy decoding.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: We expect the mixed schedule to beat both single drafters on chat and reasoning, with the best split point around a third of the block, and to add nothing on retrieval-augmented generation where lookup accepts long runs anyway. The reversed arrangement should be worse than either single drafter, which would confirm that early positions matter most.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fitting an analytical walltime model to self-derived drafters to predict cascade speedup
PROPOSAL: We characterise each training-free drafter by two measured quantities, its per-token acceptance rate against the target and its latency relative to one target forward pass, and we plug them into the expected-walltime model of cascade speculative decoding to predict the speedup of every two-level and three-level arrangement of Lookahead, SWIFT-style layer skipping, Jacobi iteration and prompt lookup. We then run the arrangements the model ranks best and worst on Llama-2-7B-chat and Mistral-7B-instruct across Spec-Bench and compare predicted with realised speedup. We optimise draft lengths per level under the model before measuring, so that the comparison is between the model's recommendation and its own expectation.
CONTROLS: Prompt lookup alone and autoregressive decoding give the floor, a brute-force grid over draft lengths for the best arrangement gives the ceiling, and we test the model's independence assumption by measuring the correlation of acceptance between consecutive draft positions. Latency is measured repeatedly per configuration and outputs are checked against greedy decoding.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: We expect the ranking of arrangements to be predicted correctly but the absolute speedup to be predicted too high for layer-skipping drafters, whose acceptance decays along the block. A large gap between the model's optimum and the grid optimum would mean that fixed-rate modelling is too coarse for self-derived drafters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early exit as a free intermediate drafter above n-gram lookup
PROPOSAL: We ask whether exiting the target large language model (LLM) at an intermediate layer, with the final normalisation and unembedding reused as they are, yields a drafter accurate enough to sit between n-gram lookup and the target. The early-exit drafter runs the lower layers only, proposes a block of tokens, and is itself drafted by prompt lookup decoding (PLD), which copies continuations of repeated n-grams from the context. We sweep the exit layer over the lower half of the eight-billion-parameter instruct version of Llama 3 and the seven-billion-parameter instruct version of Qwen 2.5, and evaluate walltime speedup on Spec-Bench and on the Grade School Math 8K (GSM8K) word problems, where lookup is known to accept little.
CONTROLS: Autoregressive decoding and PLD alone set the floor, a single-level early-exit drafter without PLD isolates the contribution of the lower level, and a cascade with the exit layer chosen at random per round checks that the exit sweep is not fitting latency noise. Draft lengths are swept for every configuration and outputs are checked for identity with greedy decoding.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: We expect an exit near the middle of the stack to give the best trade-off, with acceptance high enough on GSM8K to beat PLD alone, and shallower exits to accept too little to pay for themselves. If no exit layer beats PLD alone, intermediate-layer predictions without any trained head are too poor to serve as a cascade level.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Jacobi-style parallel decoding as the middle level of a training-free cascade
PROPOSAL: We place Jacobi iteration, which refines a whole block of guessed tokens in parallel through the target model until a fixed point, as the intermediate drafter of a cascade whose lowest level is n-gram lookup in the context: lookup seeds the initial guess of each Jacobi block, the Jacobi output becomes the draft, and the target verifies it in one pass. We run two open-weight instruction-tuned models of seven and thirteen billion parameters on Spec-Bench and on a long-document question answering set, measuring speedup over autoregressive decoding, accepted tokens per verification pass, and the number of Jacobi iterations actually spent per block.
CONTROLS: We compare against autoregressive decoding, lookup alone, Jacobi iteration seeded with the most frequent tokens instead of lookup, Lookahead decoding alone, and a cascade with a layer-skipping drafter in place of Jacobi, all with swept draft lengths and repeated timing. Every output is checked against greedy decoding of the target.
COST: 64
PREDICTION: We expect lookup seeding to cut the number of Jacobi iterations enough to make the middle level pay for itself on summarisation and retrieval-heavy inputs, and to help little on arithmetic reasoning, where the context rarely repeats. The cascade should lose to lookup alone whenever iterations exceed two per block.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online draft-length control from recent acceptance in a two-level cascade
PROPOSAL: We give each level of a cascade made of a layer-skipping self-draft above prompt lookup its own draft length, and we update both lengths during generation from an exponential moving average of the acceptance rate observed at that level: a level whose recent acceptance rises drafts longer, a level whose acceptance falls drafts shorter, with the lengths bounded between one and the block maximum. The controller amounts to a few scalar operations per round. We evaluate on Llama-2-13B-chat and Qwen2-7B-instruct across Spec-Bench, with speedup over autoregressive decoding as the primary metric and accepted tokens per round as the secondary one.
CONTROLS: Fixed draft lengths tuned by grid search per task give the strongest static comparison, fixed lengths tuned on one task and applied to the others show the price of static schedules under task shift, a controller fed random acceptance values is the placebo, and the same controller applied to single-level speculative decoding separates the gain of adaptation from the gain of cascading. Outputs are checked against greedy decoding and timings repeated.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive lengths to match the per-task grid optimum within a few percent and to beat the transferred static schedule clearly on the tasks where acceptance varies within sequences, such as multi-turn chat. The placebo controller should perform no better than the transferred schedule, otherwise the gain comes from length jitter rather than from tracking acceptance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verifying two training-free drafts in one batched target pass
PROPOSAL: Instead of choosing a drafter in advance, we let prompt lookup and a layer-skipping self-draft each propose a block for the same position, and we verify both blocks in a single batched forward pass of the target, keeping whichever block yields the longer accepted prefix. The choice is therefore made after the fact at every round, at the price of a doubled verification batch, which on memory-bound decoding adds little latency. We run Llama-3-8B-instruct and Qwen2-7B-instruct on Spec-Bench and report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding, accepted tokens per round, and how often each drafter wins per category.
CONTROLS: We compare against each drafter alone with swept draft length, against the two-level cascade of the same drafters, against an oracle that picks the better block without paying for the batched pass, and against autoregressive decoding. Outputs are checked against greedy decoding and timings repeated, including the batched pass alone to measure its overhead.
COST: 72
PREDICTION: We expect the batched verification to beat each drafter alone on every category and to beat the cascade on chat and reasoning, where the lookup block is often empty. If the batched pass takes more than a fifth longer than a single pass, the gain vanishes on the smaller model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training-free cascades under batched serving
PROPOSAL: We test whether a cascade of a layer-skipping self-draft above prompt lookup keeps its speedup when the target serves several requests at once, since draft blocks of different lengths across a batch leave verification slots unused. We run Llama-3-8B-instruct and Llama-2-13B-chat at batch sizes of one, four and sixteen with requests drawn from a mixed Spec-Bench stream, synchronising rounds across the batch and truncating every block to the length the slowest request can verify, and we measure throughput in tokens per second and per-request latency against autoregressive batched decoding and against lookup alone at the same batch size.
CONTROLS: Autoregressive decoding and lookup alone at every batch size, the cascade at batch size one as the reference, a variant that fills shorter blocks with the target's own greedy continuation, requests sorted by category versus mixed, repeated timings, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: We expect the cascade's advantage to shrink with batch size and to vanish around a batch of sixteen on the larger model, where verification stops being memory-bound. If lookup alone keeps its gain while the cascade loses it, the self-draft level is the one that fails to batch.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Which retrieval drafter belongs at the bottom of a training-free cascade
PROPOSAL: We hold the middle level fixed, a layer-skipping self-draft of Vicuna-13B and Qwen2.5-7B-instruct, and we vary the bottom level among three retrieval drafters that need no training: prompt lookup over the current context, the n-gram pool that Lookahead decoding accumulates from its own parallel branches, and a datastore of n-grams collected from the model's earlier responses to other prompts of the same category. We measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and acceptance at each level across Spec-Bench, and we test whether the bottom drafter's choice changes the best draft length of the middle level.
CONTROLS: Each bottom drafter alone without the middle level, the middle level alone, autoregressive decoding, a bottom drafter that proposes random tokens as a floor for the verification overhead, swept draft lengths for every configuration, repeated timings, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 64
PREDICTION: We expect the datastore drafter to win on retrieval-augmented generation and summarisation and prompt lookup to win on chat, with the pool drafter in between on every category. The best middle-level draft length should shorten when the bottom drafter accepts more, because the middle level then verifies longer blocks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Three-level cascade with reduced-precision drafting above lookup
PROPOSAL: We build a three-level vertical cascade for Llama-3-8B-instruct and Llama-2-13B-chat: the target in full precision verifies a draft produced by the same weights run with eight-bit activations and weights, that reduced-precision copy is drafted by a layer-skipping self-draft of the reduced-precision copy, and the bottom level is prompt lookup. No level is trained, and only the target's verification determines the output. We measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding on Spec-Bench and on a long-form summarisation set, and we vary the number of cascade rounds the lower levels run before handing a block upward.
CONTROLS: Every two-level sub-cascade and each single-level method is run with swept draft lengths, so that the gain of adding each level is isolated; autoregressive decoding and lookup alone give the floor; the reduced-precision copy used as the only drafter checks that quantisation does not degrade acceptance below the useful range. Outputs are compared token by token with greedy decoding and timings repeated.
COST: 88
PREDICTION: We expect the reduced-precision level to accept almost every token but to save too little latency per token to pay for itself on the fastest card, and the full three-level cascade to beat the best two-level one only when lower levels run a single round. If the quantised copy accepts under ninety percent of tokens, the arrangement is dominated by the two-level cascade without it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-skipping self-draft above prompt lookup on Spec-Bench
PROPOSAL: We construct a two-level cascade in which a SWIFT-style layer-skipping copy of the target drafts blocks for the target and is itself drafted by prompt lookup over n-grams of the context. We run Llama-2-13B-chat and Llama-3-8B-instruct over the six Spec-Bench categories, sweep the draft length of each level, and report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and accepted tokens per target forward pass.
CONTROLS: Autoregressive decoding as the floor, prompt lookup alone, the layer-skipping draft alone, and Lookahead decoding alone, each with its own swept draft length so that the cascade is compared with every single-level method at its best; a token-by-token identity check of all outputs against greedy decoding; repeated timings per configuration with warm caches; and a per-category breakdown so that gains on repetitive inputs do not mask losses on reasoning.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: We expect the cascade to beat lookup alone on chat, translation and reasoning and to tie on summarisation and retrieval-augmented generation. If the layer-skipping level accepts fewer than a third of its tokens, the cascade falls below lookup alone and the first question is answered negatively for this drafter.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prompt lookup under a layer-skipping self-draft across Spec-Bench
PROPOSAL: We stack prompt lookup over n-grams of the context beneath a SWIFT-style layer-skipping copy of the target, which in turn drafts for the full target. The system runs Llama-2-13B-chat and Llama-3-8B-instruct on the six Spec-Bench categories with a swept draft length per level, and we report walltime speedup over plain decoding, accepted tokens per target forward pass, and the throughput of the system in tokens per second.
CONTROLS: The cascade is run at sampling temperatures of zero and of one to check that speedup does not depend on decoding mode; peak accelerator memory is logged for every configuration; batch sizes of one, four and eight are compared; the chat template is replaced by a plain concatenation of turns to check prompt-format sensitivity; and the measured speedups are set against the figures reported in the SWIFT paper for the same models.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: We expect speedups in line with those reported for the layer-skipping method, slightly higher on the categories where lookup finds repeated n-grams. Memory should stay within a small fraction of the target model's own footprint.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Where to switch drafters inside a block, self-draft first and lookup after
PROPOSAL: Within each speculation round, an early-exit self-draft of Vicuna-7B and Llama-3-8B-instruct proposes the opening positions of the block and prompt lookup fills the remaining positions, with the switch position swept from the start to the end of the block. We measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and accepted tokens per round across Spec-Bench, and we test whether the mixed block beats either drafter used alone.
CONTROLS: Early-exit drafting alone and lookup alone at the same total block length, with their own block-length sweeps; the reversed arrangement, lookup first and self-draft after, to test that order matters in the predicted direction; a block whose drafter is drawn at random per position, as a placebo for any mixing effect; identity of outputs with greedy decoding; and repeated timings with warm caches on every configuration.
COST: 64
PREDICTION: We expect the mixed block to beat both single drafters on chat and reasoning with the switch about a third into the block, and the reversed arrangement to be worse than either, confirming that early positions carry the most value. On retrieval-augmented generation the switch should move to the start, meaning lookup alone suffices.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixed draft blocks from early-exit prediction and context lookup
PROPOSAL: An early-exit self-draft of Vicuna-7B and Llama-3-8B-instruct fills the opening positions of each draft block and prompt lookup fills the remaining ones, and we sweep the switch position from the start to the end of the block. Across Spec-Bench we measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding, accepted tokens per round, and the share of accepted tokens that came from each drafter, and we report the switch position that gives the best speedup per category.
CONTROLS: The n-gram length used by lookup is varied from two to four; the tokenizer of each model is replaced by a byte-level variant to check that acceptance is not an artefact of tokenisation; accelerator utilisation is recorded during drafting and verification; generated outputs are scored with ROUGE on summarisation and with exact match on arithmetic to confirm that quality is preserved; and the maximum generation length is varied between short and long settings.
COST: 64
PREDICTION: We expect the best switch position to lie early in the block on summarisation and later on chat and reasoning. Quality scores should match those of plain decoding on every category.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive draft lengths per cascade level from an acceptance tracker
PROPOSAL: Each level of a cascade made of Lookahead decoding above prompt lookup keeps an exponential moving average of its acceptance rate and lengthens or shortens its draft accordingly between rounds, within fixed bounds. We run Llama-2-7B-chat and Qwen2-7B-instruct on Spec-Bench and on a stream mixing prompts of all categories, and we measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and accepted tokens per round.
CONTROLS: The strongest static alternative, fixed draft lengths tuned by grid search per task with knowledge of the task label; static lengths tuned on one task and transferred to the others, which is the setting adaptation must beat; a controller fed random acceptance values, as a placebo for any effect of length jitter; the same controller on single-level speculative decoding, to separate adaptation from cascading; identity of outputs with greedy decoding; and repeated timings.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: We expect the tracker to come within a few percent of the per-task grid optimum and to beat the transferred schedule on the mixed stream. If the random-fed controller does as well, the gain comes from jitter rather than from tracking acceptance, and the second question is not answered by this mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Acceptance-driven draft-length adaptation in a two-level cascade
PROPOSAL: We let each level of a cascade that places Lookahead decoding above prompt lookup adjust its draft length between rounds from an exponential moving average of its recent acceptance rate, lengthening when acceptance rises and shortening when it falls. The system runs on Llama-2-7B-chat and Qwen2-7B-instruct over Spec-Bench and a stream that mixes prompts of all categories, and we measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding, accepted tokens per round, and the distribution of draft lengths chosen over time.
CONTROLS: The smoothing constant of the moving average is swept over four values; the warm-up length before adaptation starts is varied; the controller's own overhead is timed in isolation; accelerator memory is recorded; prompts of short and long length are evaluated separately; and the accuracy of the target model on the arithmetic category is checked against its reported value to confirm that the decoding path is correct.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: We expect draft lengths to settle quickly on each task and to vary more on the mixed stream. The controller overhead should be invisible next to a target forward pass.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Which training-free drafter earns its place above prompt lookup
PROPOSAL: We take four self-derived drafters, Lookahead decoding, SWIFT-style layer skipping, early exit at an intermediate layer, and Jacobi iteration, and we place each in turn as the middle level of a cascade whose bottom level is prompt lookup, on Mistral-7B-instruct and Llama-2-13B-chat across Spec-Bench. For each we record acceptance rate, latency relative to a target forward pass, and walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding.
CONTROLS: Lookup alone, which every cascade has to beat to be worth building; each drafter alone without lookup, which isolates what the bottom level adds; matched draft-length sweeps for every configuration; decomposition of each speedup into acceptance and relative latency, so that the reason a drafter fails is known; both model scales and all six categories, since the answer may differ by task; outputs checked against greedy decoding; repeated timings.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: We expect layer skipping and early exit to pay off on reasoning and chat, Jacobi to pay off only on repetitive inputs, and Lookahead to rarely beat lookup alone. A drafter whose relative latency exceeds a third of the target's should fail everywhere.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing self-derived drafters as the intermediate cascade level
PROPOSAL: Four training-free drafters, Lookahead decoding, SWIFT-style layer skipping, early exit from an intermediate layer, and Jacobi iteration, are each placed as the middle level of a cascade above prompt lookup, with Mistral-7B-instruct and Llama-2-13B-chat as targets, and evaluated over Spec-Bench. We record per drafter the acceptance rate, the mean draft block length actually proposed, and walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding, and we rank the drafters per category.
CONTROLS: For layer skipping the number of skipped layers is swept; the target is run in both half-precision formats to check numerical stability of verification; the perplexity of each drafter's proposals under the target is reported as a quality measure; a subsample of a quarter of the prompts per category checks that rankings are stable under fewer prompts; and the speedups are compared with the figures published for EAGLE and Medusa on the same benchmark.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: We expect layer skipping to rank first on most categories and Jacobi to rank first on summarisation. Speedups should remain below those published for the trained drafters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Predicting training-free cascade speedup from per-level acceptance and latency
PROPOSAL: We measure, for prompt lookup, layer skipping and early exit on Llama-3-8B-instruct, the acceptance rate and the latency relative to a target forward pass per Spec-Bench category, feed them to the expected-walltime model of cascade speculative decoding, and let the model choose the arrangement and draft lengths. We then run the chosen configurations and compare predicted with measured speedup.
CONTROLS: Predictions are tested on configurations the model was not fitted on, by estimating the per-level quantities on one half of the prompts and measuring speedup on the other; a brute-force grid over arrangements and draft lengths gives the true optimum against which the model's choice is judged; the independence assumption of the model is tested by measuring the correlation of acceptance between consecutive draft positions; lookup alone and autoregressive decoding set the floor; timings are repeated, and outputs are checked against greedy decoding.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: We expect the model to rank arrangements correctly and to predict speedup too high for layer skipping, whose acceptance decays along the block. If the grid optimum beats the model's choice by more than a tenth, fixed-rate modelling is too coarse for self-derived drafters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: An analytical walltime model for cascades of self-derived drafters
PROPOSAL: For prompt lookup, layer skipping and early exit on Llama-3-8B-instruct we estimate the acceptance rate and the latency relative to a target forward pass on each Spec-Bench category, and we plug the estimates into the expected-walltime model of cascade speculative decoding to compute the predicted speedup of every arrangement and draft-length setting. We then run the arrangement the model ranks first on every category and report its measured speedup next to the predicted one.
CONTROLS: The model is fitted on all prompts and its in-sample fit is reported as a coefficient of determination; the tolerance of the numerical optimiser over draft lengths is varied to check that the chosen lengths are stable; predicted speedups are tabulated for draft lengths from two to sixteen; the predicted values are set against the speedups reported in the cascade paper for trained drafters; and every estimated acceptance rate is checked to lie between zero and one.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: We expect predicted and measured speedup to agree closely on the arrangement the model ranks first. Draft lengths chosen by the optimiser should be longer for lookup than for the self-derived levels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A training-free cascade of self-draft levels above retrieval drafting
PROPOSAL: We build cascades of depth two and three in which every level above prompt lookup is a self-derived drafter of the target, a layer-skipping copy and an early-exit copy ordered by latency, so that no draft model is trained. We run Llama-2-13B-chat, Llama-3-8B-instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-instruct on Spec-Bench, sweep draft lengths per level and the number of rounds the lower levels run per upper round, and report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and acceptance per level.
CONTROLS: Lookup alone, each self-derived drafter alone, Lookahead decoding alone, autoregressive decoding, every two-level sub-cascade of the three-level one, identity of outputs with greedy decoding, and repeated timings with warm caches.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: We expect the two-level cascade to beat lookup alone on chat and reasoning, and the third level to add little because the two self-derived copies have similar acceptance. If no cascade beats lookup alone on any category, the answer to the first question is negative for current training-free drafters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A distilled compact drafter as the middle level above retrieval drafting
PROPOSAL: We distil a four-layer decoder from Llama-2-13B-chat, Llama-3-8B-instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-instruct on their own greedy outputs for the Spec-Bench prompt distribution and a general instruction corpus, initialising it from the target's embeddings and lowest layers, and we place it as the middle level of a cascade whose bottom level is prompt lookup. We sweep draft lengths per level and the number of lower-level rounds per upper round, and report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and acceptance per level.
CONTROLS: Lookup alone, the distilled drafter alone without lookup, autoregressive decoding, a distilled drafter of eight layers, identity of outputs with greedy decoding, and repeated timings with warm caches.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: We expect the distilled drafter to accept well over half of its tokens and the cascade to beat lookup alone on every category. If acceptance stays low on reasoning, more distillation data from that domain should close the gap.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-request choice of drafter above lookup from online acceptance estimates
PROPOSAL: At each speculation round a bandit chooses, for the running request, which self-derived drafter sits above prompt lookup, between layer skipping, Lookahead decoding and no middle level, with reward defined as accepted tokens per unit of measured draft latency and estimates kept per request. We run Mistral-7B-instruct and Llama-3-8B-instruct on a stream that interleaves all Spec-Bench categories, and report walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding and the share of rounds assigned to each option.
CONTROLS: The best fixed option per category with knowledge of the label as the ceiling, the best single fixed option over the whole stream as the floor adaptation must beat, a bandit choosing uniformly at random as placebo, lookup alone, identity of outputs with greedy decoding, and repeated timings.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: We expect the bandit to recover most of the gap between the single fixed option and the per-category ceiling on the mixed stream, at a small price from exploration on single-category runs. If the random bandit does as well, the gain comes from alternation and not from tracking acceptance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A per-task table of the best n-gram order for prompt lookup drafting
PROPOSAL: We study prompt lookup on its own and ask which n-gram order and which maximum draft length give the best acceptance on each Spec-Bench category for Mistral-7B-instruct and Llama-3-8B-instruct, by running every combination of n-gram orders from one to five and draft lengths from four to thirty-two offline and recording acceptance and walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding. From these runs we build a static table that assigns to each category its best lookup setting, and we evaluate the table on a stream that interleaves all categories, with the category label read from the benchmark.
CONTROLS: Lookup with a single global setting as the floor, the per-category optimum as the ceiling, identity of outputs with greedy decoding, repeated timings, and a check that the best setting is stable across the two models.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: We expect longer n-grams to win on summarisation and retrieval-augmented generation and short ones on chat, with the table beating the global setting by a modest amount. The gain should be similar on both models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tracking acceptance drift along responses to time the drafter switch
PROPOSAL: We log, on Spec-Bench with Vicuna-13B and Qwen2.5-7B-instruct, the acceptance of prompt lookup and of a layer-skipping self-draft at every position of every response, fit a schedule that picks the drafter and draft length per position range to maximise accepted tokens per unit latency, and deploy it in a cascade that switches drafter as the response advances.
CONTROLS: The best fixed cascade with one drafter assignment, lookup alone, autoregressive decoding, a schedule fitted on shuffled traces as placebo, fitting on half of the prompts per category and evaluating on the other half, repeated timings, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: We expect lookup acceptance to rise along long responses as they start repeating themselves and self-draft acceptance to stay flat, so the fitted schedule hands over to lookup partway through and gains most on summarisation and multi-turn chat. The placebo schedule should not beat the fixed cascade.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Checking output fidelity of training-free cascades across tasks
PROPOSAL: We run a cascade of a layer-skipping self-draft above prompt lookup on Vicuna-13B and Qwen2.5-7B-instruct over Spec-Bench and compare its outputs with those of standard decoding under greedy and under sampling at temperature one with a shared random state, measuring exact token agreement, ROUGE on summarisation, BLEU on translation, exact-match accuracy on arithmetic, and answer overlap on question answering, to establish on which categories the cascade preserves quality.
CONTROLS: Standard decoding of each target run twice with the same random state to measure the agreement ceiling, lookup alone, the self-draft alone, three draft lengths per level, and a tally of positions where draft and target disagreed.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: We expect token agreement at the ceiling under greedy decoding and slightly below it under sampling because of floating-point ordering, with task metrics unchanged on every category. Any category with lower agreement would point to a verification bug.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Choosing cascade schedules per accelerator from measured drafter profiles
PROPOSAL: We profile prompt lookup, layer skipping and early exit on Llama-2-7B-chat and Llama-3-8B-instruct on a data-centre card, an older data-centre card and a consumer card, recording acceptance and latency relative to a target forward pass, then select for each card the cascade arrangement and draft lengths that the expected-walltime model ranks first, and measure the speedup of each selected schedule on its own card and on the other cards over Spec-Bench.
CONTROLS: Lookup alone and autoregressive decoding on every card, a brute-force grid per card to check the model's choice, fixed kernels and precision across cards, repeated timings with warm caches, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 72
PREDICTION: We expect the self-draft level to pay on the consumer card, where memory bandwidth dominates and skipping layers saves proportionally more, and not on the fastest card. A schedule transferred from another card should lose a modest share of the speedup, most when moving to the consumer card.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fused verification kernels to shorten the target's forward pass in cascades
PROPOSAL: We profile the verification pass of Llama-2-7B-chat and Llama-3-8B-instruct inside a cascade of layer skipping above prompt lookup on a data-centre card, an older data-centre card and a consumer card, attribute its latency to attention, feed-forward and sampling kernels, and then implement a fused attention-and-sampling kernel for the tree-shaped verification of draft blocks together with a cache layout that avoids re-copying rejected positions. We measure the latency of the verification pass per draft length and the resulting end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding across Spec-Bench.
CONTROLS: The unfused verification pass on every card, the cascade with the original cache layout, repeated timings with warm caches, fixed precision across cards, and identity of outputs with greedy decoding.
COST: 72
